observations: The overview evaluates muscle size, strength, power, endurance and physical-function outcomes separately.
An outcome-specific result should not be presented as improvement in every performance domain.
The discussion describes weekly volume load using load per repetition, repetitions per set, sets per exercise, exercises per session and sessions per week.
Weekly volume load was rarely considered in the included reviews.
The discussion describes an inverse relationship between repetitions and load when a given load and near-fatiguing effort are applied.
Conversions between repetition maximum and percentage of one-repetition maximum can vary by exercise and between people.
The discussion describes increasing absolute load in line with strength gains, using regular strength testing or perceived-exertion information.
Increasing stimulus is discussed for continued longer-term progress; progression is not required for every beneficial outcome reported in the overview.
The discussion reports that more sets can support strength and hypertrophy, while the exact number needed to optimize adaptation could not be determined.
The authors hypothesize diminishing additional benefit as further sets are added.
The discussion describes variation as systematic modification of resistance-training variables and periodization as one common form.
Definitions of periodization differ, and its ordering of variables for particular goals may be understudied relative to the overview outcomes.
Unless otherwise specified, the overview measured strength as voluntary isotonic one-repetition maximum in the same mode as the training.
The discussion notes exercise-specific and between-person variation in conversions between percentage of one-repetition maximum and repetition maximum.
Weekly volume load was rarely considered in the reviews included in this overview.
The discussion evaluates set volume separately and states that the exact number of sets required to optimize adaptation could not be ascertained.
